title: Stop Lecturing Students And Lower Your Stress tudents-and-lower-your-stress/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin connects two common classroom sights -- teachers lecturing individual misbehaving students and stressed-out, burned-out teachers -- arguing that the first is a leading cause of the second. He contends that relying on words, persuasion, and one-on-one 'talking to's to change behavior is an exhausting, uphill battle that rarely produces lasting change and instead functions, in students' eyes, as the actual consequence itself, meaning that if a student can simply endure the lecture, no further consequence follows. He warns that lecturing often devolves into interrogation ('why did you do that?'), which is largely pointless since most people, adults included, cannot articulate why they made a bad choice, and that pressing for answers risks provoking arguments that erode a teacher's authority. He distinguishes this from whole-class talks or genuine praise, which he considers legitimate uses of words, and insists that individual behavioral lectures should be replaced entirely by consistent enforcement of a classroom management plan's stated consequences. The piece closes by tying this shift directly to reduced teacher stress, framing plan-following as both more effective and less emotionally taxing than lecturing.
points: Lecturing individual misbehaving students is identified as a leading, underrecognized cause of teacher stress and burnout.
Students often experience a one-on-one lecture as the consequence itself -- if they can 'weather' the lecture, they expect no further consequence to follow.
Interrogating students about why they misbehaved is largely futile, since most people cannot articulate the reasons behind a bad choice, and pushing for answers risks provoking arguments.
Arguing with a student lowers a teacher's leadership stature to the student's level, undermining classroom authority.
Replacing individual lecturing with consistent enforcement of stated consequences is presented as both more effective for changing behavior and less stressful for teachers.
quotes: It is my belief that the number one cause of stress among teachers is a reliance on one’s words to try to convince students to behave as desired—i.e., lecturing students as a method of classroom management.
Lecturing individual students isn’t an effective classroom management strategy because it doesn’t work in the long run, it creates resentment in your students, and it’s stressful to you.
Listening to your criticism is the consequence. If they can weather your lecture, they know they will be free from further consequence when it’s over.
Why a student breaks a rule is, in most circumstances, irrelevant. Very few students, or adults for that matter, are able to articulate why they made a bad choice.
Arguing with students lowers your leadership stature and authority to the same level of the student—which it is not. You are the teacher and leader in the classroom and you make the decisions.
Rules are rules. Other than for the purpose of gathering information, there is nothing to talk about. If a student breaks a rule, you give him or her a consequence and move on.
What does work is following your classroom management plan exclusively. Lecturing doesn’t support your plan; it hinders it.
